newsitem.title: MEXICO: Ortiz says Mexico savings rate above 20 pct of GDP.
newsitem.headline: Ortiz says Mexico savings rate above 20 pct of GDP.

text.p: Mexico's national savings rate rose above 20 percent of Gross Domestic Product in 1996, but for strong medium-term growth rates it needs to exceed 25 percent, Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz said on Tuesday.
He said savings jumped from 15 percent to 20 percent of
GDP in 1995, but he painted the rise as a mixed blessing because it occurred in a year of economic crisis when consumption fell even more than the nation's revenues.

"In 1996, there was a more healthy savings increase because national income grew 4.5 percent, while consumption grew less," Ortiz was quoted by the Finance Ministry as saying during a tour of the central state of Queretaro.
"But if Mexico aspires to growth rates of six percent in its GDP in the medium term, it needs to reach coefficient rates of domestic savings above 25 percent," he said.

Mexico plans to introduce privately-run pension systems later this year, which it hopes will boost savings. Ortiz said the pension reforms would generate long-term savings for the first time that he said would be invested in projects with a long maturity span, such as infrastructure and housing.

Seperately, he said that Mexico was expected to report a health fiscal surplus in 1996, largely because of higher-than expected oil prices last year. Part of the surplus, he added, would be transferred to the Bank Insurance Fund (Fobaproa) and used to help prop up the country's shaky financial system.
